summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for monitoring and controlling network devices with APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking) capabilities, using SMIv2. It was replaced by RFC 2455.

eli5.summary: A set of standard dials for checking an older IBM-style network.

questions: snmp objects for advanced peer-to-peer networking
how do i monitor appn networks with snmp
what is a transmission group in appn
subtitle: Management objects for IBM's Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking.

tldr.problem: APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking) nodes and networks need to be monitored and managed, but no standard management objects existed for them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a comprehensive set of SNMP MIB objects in SMIv2 that allow network management stations to monitor APPN node status, configuration, ports, link stations, network topology, and directory information.
tldr.outcome: APPN networks can now be managed via standard SNMP, providing visibility into node behavior, topology, routing, and performance. RFC 2455 later replaces this with an update.

facts.label: Node types defined
facts.value: Network nodes, end nodes, virtual routing nodes

today: RFC 2155 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2455. APPN networks are now primarily found only in legacy IBM mainframe environments and are no longer deployed in modern networks. For organizations still operating APPN, the successor MIB provides the updated management approach.

sections.title: Introduction and APPN Basics
sections.content:
APPN is the peer-to-peer networking aspect of IBM's Systems Network Architecture (SNA). Unlike traditional SNA where mainframes control everything, APPN allows network nodes to discover routes and establish sessions dynamically without central control. An APPN network consists of different types of nodes: network nodes (NNs) that route and manage the network, end nodes (ENs) that are session endpoints, and virtual routing nodes (VRNs) that represent shared facilities like LANs.

Each APPN node maintains several databases: a network topology database that maps the nodes and transmission groups (links) in the network, a directory database that tracks where logical units (LUs) are located, and a class-of-service database that associates routing costs with different service levels. Transmission groups connect nodes and are the basic data-carrying links.

This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) using the SNMPv2 SMI so that management stations can monitor and control APPN networks via SNMP.
sections.eli5: APPN is like a cooperative network where different computers find and talk to each other without a boss. The MIB is the checklist for a manager to see what each computer is doing.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Groups
sections.content:
The APPN MIB is organized into seven major groups of managed objects. The appnNode group covers information about the local APPN node itself, including general node characteristics, port configuration, and link station status. The appnNn group, present only on network nodes, represents the network topology database that the node maintains: the NNs, VRNs, and transmission groups that make up the known network.

The appnLocalTopology group represents the local topology information known to any APPN node. The appnDir group covers the directory database, which lists logical units and which node owns each one. The appnCos group defines class-of-service information, including how service levels map to routing weights. The appnSessIntermediate group tracks intermediate sessions that pass through this node as a transit point.

Finally, appnTraps define SNMP notifications for SNA Management Services alert conditions. The MIB is comprehensive but excludes endpoint session management, dependent LU requester functionality, and high-performance routing extensions, which are defined in separate MIBs.
sections.eli5: The MIB divides APPN management into sections: the local node itself, the big picture of the network, where resources are located, how traffic is prioritized, and what went wrong.

sections.title: Monitoring Nodes, Ports, and Link Stations
sections.content:
The appnNode group allows a manager to monitor the state and configuration of APPN ports and link stations on any APPN node. Each port has configuration parameters (DLC type, port state), and each link station has configuration parameters and status information including the state of the link to an adjacent node.

The appnLsStatusTable records historical error information from link station connection attempts and disconnections, capturing sense data that explains why connections failed. This allows troubleshooting of network connectivity problems. Network nodes also report node-specific information such as routing characteristics.

Management stations can use this information to activate and deactivate ports and link stations, monitor their status, and correlate connection failures with network issues.
sections.eli5: Managers can see if ports are plugged in and working, whether cables are connected to neighbors, and get error codes when something breaks.

sections.title: Network Topology and Routing Information
sections.content:
Network nodes maintain a replicated network topology database that is exchanged with other network nodes over control-point-to-control-point (CP-CP) sessions. The appnNn group exposes this topology information via the appnNnTopology table, which lists network nodes, virtual routing nodes, and transmission groups between them.

The topology database entries are indexed by a flow reduction sequence number (FRSN), which allows management stations to retrieve only incremental updates rather than the entire database each time. This is important for scalability in large networks. The database includes state and routing characteristics for each transmission group, such as effective capacity and available bandwidth.

The appnLocalTopology group provides similar topology information for the local node's view, including transmission groups to end nodes learned through end-node registration. Each network node also maintains a class-of-service database that assigns routing weights to resources for different service levels, enabling class-based routing.
sections.eli5: Managers can see the map of the network: which nodes can reach which nodes, how fast each connection is, and how good they are for different types of traffic.

sections.title: Directory Database and Service Discovery
sections.content:
APPN nodes maintain a directory database that tracks the location of logical units (LUs), which are the actual session endpoints that applications use. Directory information is learned from three sources: local LU definitions, LU registration from end nodes served by this network node, and LUs discovered via network searches from other nodes.

The appnDir group exposes directory entries and performance information about directory operations. A management station can see which LUs are known to a node, which node owns each LU, and which serving network node manages that owning node. This information is essential for understanding where sessions can be established.

The MIB also tracks directory performance metrics, including information about directory searches and their results. The appnSessIntermediate group complements this by tracking intermediate sessions that are currently active through the node, including route selection control vectors that describe the service level and path taken by each session.
sections.eli5: The directory is a phonebook that says where each service is located. Managers can see if new services have been registered and how fast the network finds them.

sections.title: Status and Obsolescence
sections.content:
This RFC defines a comprehensive and detailed management infrastructure for APPN networks. However, APPN itself has become obsolete with the rise of IP-based networking. This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 2455, which provides an updated version of the MIB.

APPN and SNA are primarily found in legacy IBM mainframe environments and are no longer deployed in new networks. However, for organizations with existing APPN networks, this MIB remains a useful management tool for monitoring and troubleshooting network operation.
sections.eli5: This MIB was the way to manage APPN networks when they were common. Now those networks are mainly in old systems, and IP networks have taken over.
